Okay so, Shiftwell. This is the most recent real job, before I took the time off for my dad. Shiftwell does scheduling and time tracking and HR stuff for hourly workforces, so think restaurants, urgent care clinics, a lot of retail. Managers build the schedule, people swap shifts on their phones, and then all of that feeds into payroll. It was maybe 250 people when I joined, something like 70 engineers, headquartered in Austin but a lot of people were remote.

I started there in October 2018. I'm pretty sure it was October, because my first week was the week they did the big Halloween thing in the office and I didn't know anybody and I was the only one not in a costume. Came in as a senior backend engineer. Got promoted to staff engineer in 2021, I think the spring cycle.

The big thing, the thing I'd actually want somebody to know about, is the monolith work. Shiftwell was one giant Rails app. Everything was in it. Scheduling, time off, payroll exports, notifications, the auth stuff, all of it. And honestly it worked fine for years, but by 2019 deploys were taking like 45 minutes, and if anything broke in, say, notifications, it could take down the scheduling screens, which is the thing managers are staring at at 6am trying to figure out who's covering the breakfast shift. So I wrote up a proposal, kind of a strangler pattern thing, pull pieces out one at a time behind the existing APIs so the mobile apps don't even know, and leadership said okay, go.

I pretty much rewrote the whole platform over the next couple years. I mean, okay, to be fair, what we actually did was pull five services out. Time-off accruals was first, because the accrual math was a mess and it was well contained. Then payroll export, then notifications, then the scheduling rules engine, which was the scary one, and then the integrations gateway that talked to the payroll providers. All in Go, Postgres behind each one, events over Kafka, because I knew Kafka from Tallyline and I knew where the bodies were buried with it. The Rails app is still there, it still does a lot. It's still most of the product, honestly. But the parts that hurt the most got pulled out.

I was the tech lead for that. It was me and six engineers most of the time, it shifted a bit as people moved around. I wasn't their manager, I want to be clear about that, nobody reported to me. I did the designs, the code reviews, ran the weekly architecture sync, paired a lot, especially with the two junior folks.

Numbers I remember. The payroll export used to be a nightly job that ran about six hours, and customers on the east coast would sometimes not have their file by morning, which, when it's payroll, people get very upset. After we moved it into its own service and made it incremental, so it only recomputes what changed, it was around forty minutes. Deploys for the extracted services went down to about twelve minutes, versus the 45 for the monolith. And the accruals bugs, we used to get, I want to say, 30 or 40 support tickets a month about wrong PTO balances, and after the rewrite it was like a handful. Single digits.

The accruals thing was funny because it's basically a ledger. Hours earned, hours used, carryover, expirations, it's double-entry if you squint. So I kind of brought the Tallyline ledger thinking over: every balance change is an entry, you never update a balance in place, and you can always explain why someone has 31.5 hours. That's what fixed the tickets really. Not anything fancy.

Around 2022 my director asked if I wanted to move into management, take over the platform team as the engineering manager. And I thought about it, I really did, for like a month. But I said no, not yet. I like being the person who's in the code and in the design docs. I mentored a couple of people through promotion to senior, which I loved, so maybe someday. Not then, and honestly not right now either.

Anyway. Other stuff. I was on the on-call rotation the whole time, one week in about eight. I ran the incident review process for a while and wrote the postmortem template we used. Did a lot of interviewing, probably over a hundred interviews over the four-plus years. I also pushed us onto Kubernetes for the new services, which was its own adventure.

I left in April 2023. My dad had his stroke in January, and I was flying back and forth to Atlanta for a few months trying to make it work, and it just didn't. Shiftwell was really good about it, they gave me leave first, but in the end I resigned. I'd do it again. Left on good terms, and my old director said he'd be a reference anytime.
